subject: DCCN
summaries:
802.11 Wireless LAN provides network connectivity over wireless media. 
      An Access Point (AP) acts as a bridge between wireless and wired networks. 
      The AP is connected to a wired network and has antennae for wireless connectivity. 
      Key devices include: 
      * Desktop with PCI 802.11 LAN card 
      * Laptop with PCMCIA 802.11 LAN card 
      * Access Point 
      The range of 802.11 Wireless LAN depends on structural hindrances and RF gain of the antenna. 
      Multiple APs may be installed with a 20-30% overlap to service larger areas. 
      A client is always associated with one AP and performs a Hand-Off when moving to another AP. 
      There are three flavors of 802.11: 
      * 802.11b 
      * 802.11a 
      * 802.11g 
      Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance (MACA) is used for data transmission, involving: 
      * Request to Send (RTS) frame 
      * Clear to Send (CTS) frame 
      * Data transmission 
      * ACK frame 
      WLAN standards include: 
      * 802.11b: supports 1, 2, 5.5, and 11 Mbps in the 2.4 GHz ISM band 
      * 802.11a: operates in the 5 GHz UNII band, supports up to 54 Mbps 
      * 802.11g: supports up to 54 Mbps in the 2.4 GHz band, backward compatible with 802.11b 
      Categories of wireless networks include: 
      * Base Station: all communication through an access point 
      * Infrastructure Wireless: base station network connected to the wired Internet 
      * Ad hoc Wireless: wireless nodes communicate directly 
      * MANETs (Mobile Ad Hoc Networks): ad hoc nodes are mobile
